Retail investors are extremely bullish:

Allocation to stocks among retail investors in the AAII survey rose +0.7 percentage points in September, to 71.8%, the highest level since December 2017.

This also marks its 2nd-highest reading since July 2000.

Since April, this figure has risen +3.3 percentage points, its largest 5-month increase since October 2025.

To put this into perspective, average retail exposure to stocks since 1987 is 71.8%.

Meanwhile, allocation to cash fell -1.0 percentage point last month to 13.3%, its lowest since December 2017.

At the same time, allocation to bonds rose +0.3 percentage points, to 14.9%, remaining below its average of 15.9% since 1987.

Appetite for risk among retail investors is through the roof.

BREAKING: The "AI Big 10" now accounts for a record 42% of US stock market cap.

This includes Magnificent 7 stocks as well as Broadcom, $AVGO, AMD, $AMD, and Micron, $MU.

This figure has more than doubled since the 2022 bear market low.

By comparison, during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble, the Technology, Media & Telecom (TMT) sector peaked at 41%, while the Nifty Fifty peaked at 40% in the 1970s.

Furthermore, Japan’s equity market bubble in the 1980s peaked at 44%.

In the past, only railroad stocks have significantly exceeded this concentration, accounting for 63% of US market cap at their highest point in the 1900s.

The dominance of Big Tech is extraordinary.

With trailing earnings up 28% and forward earnings expected to grow another 20%, it’s understandable that investors don’t want to pay high multiples. The market’s trailing P/E multiple is down 10% year-over-year. History shows that investors don’t tend to pay top multiples for peak earnings growth. 🧵(2/2)

One thing I find interesting is that there’s a widespread narrative out there that real rates are rising in part because the US economy is running hot. It seems plausible, except that (aside from the strong PMIs) I don’t see much evidence of it in the chart below. The squiggles at the bottom show Bloomberg’s GDP surveys. Estimated real GDP growth rates for 2026-2028 are decent (2.1-2.2%) but hardly booming, and they are not even at the real potential growth rate. My guess is that the main culprit behind the rise in real yields is fiscal risk, amplified by crowding out and convexity hedging.

BREAKING: Broadcom, $AVGO, is seeking more than $50 billion in financing for OpenAI’s custom AI chip, which the firms are developing together, per WSJ.

Apollo and Blackstone are among the lenders Broadcom has talked to about participating in the deal.

The financing is intended to help Oracle bridge the gap between when it has to pay for the hardware and when its cloud computing revenue starts coming in.

BREAKING: Global central banks acquired +39 tonnes of gold in August, marking their 5th consecutive monthly purchase.

This follows +23 tonnes in July and +52 tonnes in June.

China again led demand, adding +20 tonnes and bringing its year-to-date purchases to +80 tonnes.

China’s official gold reserves have now risen to a record 2,387 tonnes, or 9% of its total FX reserves.

Furthermore, Poland bought +8 tonnes, lifting its year-to-date purchases to +98 tonnes and total gold reserves to a record 648 tonnes.

So far in 2026, central banks have acquired +170 tonnes of gold.

Central banks continue to aggressively accumulate gold.
